Milkeyway - thank you very much for stopping my my journal! Its an honor to have an associate trader taking the time to post here!

Your chart is very enlightening. Here are the key parts I am noticing:

1. This bullish QM is forming at a S/R level. I labeled the S/R as ("1"). I wonder if QM's work better when they form at major S/R levels?.... seems logical to me. 2. There is a FTR that formed before the initial break of the S/R (I labeled this FTR "2"). 3. Price then moves down and back up through the S/R level and engulfs the FTR 2 ( I labeled this FTR "3"). This should be an indication to a trader that a QM may be forming at an important level. 4. Price moves back towards the S/R level before taking off and making new highs. This final retrace also forms an important FTR and becomes the origin of the bullish push up (4). 5. I labeled the LL of the QM as "A"

mentioned in his journal: "the usable engulf is the engulf that hasn't hit its target". This was also enlightening for me because I didn't realize engulfs always had a target... I just usually placed a target after getting in to a trade at the base of a pole of an important S/R level.

In your example, an engulf of the FTR 2 (the source of the original break of the S/R) occurs, and I would say its target is the spot where I labeled on the chart (not sure if this is accurate).

Three Main Questions: 1. Is the FTR (where you also label 'origin') the origin of the big bullish up move, or is it considered to be the origin of the engulf? I always thought (see label "A") was the origin of the engulf.

2. If you were trading this chart live, where would you have looked to enter? I noticed the FTR (Labeled 4) retraced back to a spot just under the S/R, but I don't see any glaring reason why price decided to move up from that point. Is there a way a sharp trader would have known that the #4 would retrace exactly to that level, or would you be gradually buying in to the move as price retraced closer to "A"? I would have put a stop just under "A".

3. Would trading the FTB to the FTR/Origin (labeled 4) be a good trade? It seems like a FTB to this zone would be very reactive.

Again, thank you very much for helping me out. Your time spent here is genuinely appreciated. Feel free to ignore any questions you don't want to answer.

:)

Hi Keyador!

I definitely didn't see that flag. I should have gone to a lower time frame. Would you say the engulf needs to be of the original flag? In other words, if a flag has been visited by price (FTB), whether there is a future engulf is not whether the flag created by the FTB is engulfed, but the original flag that the FTB flag was reacting to is engulfed?

If this statement is true, then you have really helped me pass a milestone in understanding the concept of the engulf. This could explain many failed trades where I thought there was an engulf, but really the flag I was thinking got engulfed was just a reaction to the original flag (further left).

This is difficult to explain using words. Here is a drawing I made to better illustrate my question:

Is it true that:

#1 is the original flag. It is this flag that matters when it comes to engulfing #2 is not the original flag. It is a reaction (FTB) to the original flag. "A" is not a true engulf (this is the mistake I made of GBP/CAD). It looks like an engulf, but if you look further left you will see #1 is the true flag that matters. "B" is a true engulf of # 1 and is a move that can be traded accordingly.

My interpretation of this diagram (from Milkeyway, follow link on Post # 85)

#1 – Is an FTR which occurs after engulf “A”, and is the origin of the engulf “B”. #2- Is an FTR which occurs after the engulf “B” and is the origin of the engulf “C”. “D” is an engulf of FTR “2”, and is a FTB to FTR “1” #3 is an FTR, but it is also the target of traders who took a Long trade on price’s FTB to FTR “1”. FTR 3 is the Target of long trades from the FTB to FTR “1” because of the S/R level as shown on the diagram. It is also the QM level where we would expect sellers to jump in. This is also near the origin of the engulf “D”. FTR 3 is an important level, and is an area where I should start anticipating a PAZ forming. FTR #3 is the origin of the down move where price engulfs “E”. FTR #4 forms and also serves as the origin of the next down move. FTR #4 is the target of sellers who took shorts at FTR #3. PAZ formed between FTR #3 and FTR #4. Wait for price to enter in to this PAZ zone and only trade the edges.

Only question I have: why was FTR #4 the target of the traders who went short at FTR #3? Wouldn’t the target be the red rectangle (I drew it too short, but assume it extends fully to the right) closer to the area when “E” engulf occurred? Why would I wait for the pull back and formation of FTR #4? Wouldn’t it make sense to just stay in the trade since Engulf “E” occurred to the downside indicating a further price drop?

Thanks Keyador, I've drawn a bit more on the diagram to see if I am on the right path.

Here's what I see:

Price reaches the important flag on its first time back. Price reacts a little but ultimately engulfs the flag. Price then retraces a bit before creating a new high (creating FTR #1). This FTR #1 is important because it is the zone where price retraced and broke the original important flag to the left. When price engulfs FTR # 1 again (where you labeled the engulf) it is significant because it broke the FTR that formed after the break of the original important flag (left).

Here's a topic I need to refresh my memory on...

Difference between a flag and a FTR:

An 'FTR' forms after price breaks an important S/R zone. Flag limits just mark the high and low of a brief indecision in price. Flags are DBD and RBR. FTR's are found within flags, but not every flag has an FTR within it.

In this diagram from Marketpedia I drew in black rectangles to show all of the flag limits.

Hopefully this is accurate...
